title: How to read a studio portfolio
metaTitle: What to look for in a portfolio
excerpt: Read a studio portfolio for the decision, the constraint, and a sentence that could only belong to that project. A pretty frame without that sentence is not evidence.
primaryKeyword: how to review a design portfolio
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a finished room that still needs a sentence about why it was made that way.
caption: A finished room between two windows. A portfolio still needs the decision, not only the frame. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should you look for in a studio portfolio?
faqs.answer: Look for the constraint, the decision, and whether the work could have been made for anyone. A useful case includes a choice a serious person might have made differently. A gallery of heroes with no sentence about what was refused is a brochure.

faqs.question: Can a portfolio prove the studio will be easy to work with?
faqs.answer: It cannot. The frames show the output, not the late disagreement or the way scope was handled. Use the portfolio to test judgment, then use the first call to ask who decides, what you will own, and what done means.

faqs.question: Should awards and revenue numbers decide the hire?
faqs.answer: Treat them as a footnote. Ask what a number measured and who measured it. The constraint and the choice transfer to your project more reliably than a trophy or an unexplained result.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Read a studio portfolio for the decision, the constraint, and the sentence that could only belong to that project. Pretty frames are pleasant. They are not evidence. How to review a design portfolio is mostly the discipline of asking what changed for the client, and what the studio refused to do.

Give each project two minutes of honesty before you fall in love with the type. You are hiring a judgment. The pictures are how that judgment left a trace.

## Start with the sentence, not the crop

Open one project. Before you scroll, look for a sentence that says what was wrong, what was decided, and what the work had to respect. A restructure of a shop. A heritage archive that had to read on a phone. A product that had to be scannable by a busy operator. If the only sentences are "we crafted a digital experience," close the project and open another.

The sentence should name a constraint that pinched. Time, a legacy catalog, a brand that could not be thrown away, a regulator, a warehouse, a community that already had a name for itself. Work without a constraint could have been made for anyone. Work that names a constraint can be compared to your constraint.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a page shows first-hand experience, and whether a reader can tell who did the work. A portfolio page is that test in public. Photographs of the outcome, notes on the decision, and a clear studio name are the marks of experience. A mood film with no decision is an ad for the studio's taste. Taste is real. It does not tell you how they behave when the catalog is messy.

Hanabi's public projects can be read this way, and so can anyone else's. Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign. The question to ask of a case like that is what moved, what stayed, and how a shopper still understood the store. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site. The question is how the craft and the archive survived contact with a modern page. If a studio's own case cannot support those questions, assume your case will be a gallery too.

## Look for a decision you can disagree with

A useful case includes a choice a serious person might have made differently. One type pair instead of three. A shop path separated from a visit path. A homepage written for the buyer who pays, with other audiences given a link. Navigation cut in half. A feature left out of the first release.

If every choice is described as inevitable and brilliant, you are reading a brochure. Ask, in the call, what they almost did and why they did not. The answer matters more than the mockup. A studio that can narrate a rejected direction understands the work. A studio that has only the final pixels may have received them from the client intact.

Look at what is absent. Empty states. A form. A plain page with a lot of text. Mobile. If the portfolio only shows the hero at desktop, you do not yet know whether the studio can finish a page. Beautiful heroes are the easy part. The supplier page, the error, and the footer are where judgment shows.

Compare two projects by the same studio. Do they look identical with the logo swapped? Range can mean skill. It can also mean no point of view. You want a recognizable standard of clarity applied to different problems, not one template and not a new personality every time. Wabisabi and Ballarat Box Sports should not look like the same mood. They should both look considered. That is the distinction.

## Separate the studio's work from the client's assets

A luxury photograph can make an average site look expensive. Ask what the studio made and what they were given. The words. The structure. The product interface. The identity. The build.

A case that says "brand and website" should let you see both. If you only see a homepage, you do not know whether there is a system underneath. Ask to see a second page, a component, or the type in a dull context, like an email or a packing note. Systems reveal themselves where glamour is hard.

If the studio both designs and builds, look for signs the build is real. A link to the live site. A note about the stack only if it mattered. Performance, accessibility, and a CMS the client can edit are legitimate parts of a case. They should be described in human language. "Built on Next.js" is a fact. It is not a result. The result is a shopper finishing a purchase, or an editor publishing a page without a ticket.

Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are public product examples. Read product shots for hierarchy, not for glow. Can you tell what to do first? Are the labels verbs a person would say? Trade Moai's value, as an interface, is that a person can scan. If a portfolio product shot cannot be scanned, the glow is doing the selling.

Ask whose words are on the site. Many weak portfolios are strong art direction on client copy that was already clear. That is a fine service. It is a different service from finding the sentence. You need to know which one you are buying.

## What a frame cannot prove

A frame cannot prove the working relationship. You will not see the late disagreement, the scope swap, or the way they talk to a nervous founder. That is what the first call is for. The portfolio can only show whether the output of those relationships contains decisions.

A frame cannot prove results the studio does not have. Be wary of revenue claims, award stacks, and timelines with no source. You do not need them. You need the constraint and the choice. If a number is offered, ask what it measured and who measured it. Invented precision is a reason to slow down.

A frame cannot prove that the work will match your industry. A studio can learn a new domain. What transfers is the quality of attention: structure, type, a sentence, a build the client owns. What does not transfer automatically is your customer's vocabulary. Look for at least one project where they had to learn a vocabulary that was not their own, and where the words on the site sound like the customer, not like a keynote.

Awards and press logos are optional. They are easy to fake in spirit even when the award is real, because the award often judges the frame. Use them as a footnote. Use the case as the page.

## How to read the studio's own site

The studio's site is a portfolio item they fully control. Read it with the same questions. Is the offer clear in the first screen? Is there proof with a constraint? Can you tell who does the work? Is there a way to start that matches the offer?

A studio site that is only a reel, with no sentences, is telling you how they will treat your content. A studio site that explains the services, the work, and the next step is telling you they can do the unglamorous part. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the kind of index this piece is arguing for: projects you can open, with a point of view, rather than a grid of untitled crops.

Check the basics while you are there. Can you read the type on a phone? Does the page jump while loading? Do you know what to click? You are not running an audit. You are noticing whether they hold themselves to the standard they will sell you. Nielsen Norman Group's observation still applies: people decide quickly, often in 10 to 20 seconds, whether a page deserves more time. If the studio's own homepage fails that test, believe it.

Look at the writing. Short, specific, and willing to say no is a good sign. A fog of "elevate, seamless, bespoke" is a sign that your pages will sound like that too, unless you bring every sentence yourself. Sometimes that is the deal. Know if it is.

## Questions to carry into the next conversation

Pick two projects and ask the same three questions of each. What was the constraint? What did you decide? What did the client own at the end? Listen for concrete nouns. Pages, states, a repo, a portal, a catalog, a typeface with a license.

Ask what they would do differently now. A studio that has only praise for its old work has stopped looking. A studio that can name one change, without trashing the client, is still practicing.

Ask which project is closest to yours, and why. The honest answer is sometimes "none, and here is the part that still applies." That answer is better than a forced twin. You are listening for judgment.

Then ask what a first release would leave out. Portfolios show the end state. Your risk is the middle. A studio that can describe a smaller first ship is a studio that can scope. The piece on [a scope that survives the first client meeting](/blog/a-scope-that-survives-the-first-client-meeting) is the next read, because a beautiful case history will not protect you from a vague statement of work.

Bring those two projects to the conversation. Point at the sentence you believed, and at the sentence you did not. A studio that can talk about both is worth a second meeting.
